\subsection{AMD XDNA~2 NPU}
\label{subsec:platform}

% VALUE: the array: 8 columns of shim, memory and core tiles; DMAs follow chained BDs on channels with task queues, locks hand buffers over, routes cross switches whose ports buffer data; a configuration and a design; once configured, each operator's group of tiles computes independently, and its columns are its column group
% SOURCE: the XDNA 2 topology is the kernel documentation's, which states 4 rows of compute tiles in 8 columns, 1 memory-tile row per column, and 4,096 KB of L2 (docs.kernel.org/accel/amdxdna/amdnpu.html, read 2026-10-21). Confirmed on the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 NPU of this paper's machine. Rico et al. (IEEE Micro 2024) is the first XDNA generation (5 columns) and is not cited for an XDNA 2 figure.
% SOURCE: tile anatomy, DMA channels with task queues (pp. 24, 35, 59), and the stream switch with its ports (pp. 18-19) (AM027 v1.1).
% DECISION: column groups are how today's LLM designs map their flows, not a hardware rule (author, 2026-10-24).
\textbf{AI Engine Array.}
An AMD XDNA~2 NPU is a spatial dataflow array of AI Engine (AIE) tiles in 8 columns~\citep{linux-amdnpu}.
Each column holds a shim tile that reaches DRAM, a memory tile, and 4 core tiles with local memory.
Direct memory access (DMA) engines move data by following buffer descriptors (BDs), which can chain, and locks hand each buffer from its producer to its consumer~\citep{amd_am027}.
Each DMA channel takes its work from its own \emph{task queue}, and data travels between tiles on \emph{routes} through the tiles' stream switches, whose ports buffer data in flight.
A \emph{configuration} of the array is its core programs, stream routes, BDs, and locks, which a compiler such as MLIR-AIE~\citep{mlir-aie-repo} or MLIR-AIR (AIR)~\citep{wang2026mlirair} emits, and a \emph{design} is one or more configurations with the host program that issues their dispatches.
The configured array runs data-driven, so a design maps each operator's flow onto a group of tiles that computes independently whenever its input locks are released.
We call the columns that one operator occupies its \emph{column group}.

% VALUE: the CP: a dispatch's instruction stream runs in order; issue returns at once, a synchronization blocks; so the CP's order decides when each column group gets work, and with nothing reordering across engines that order is the array's schedule (measured in Section 3)
% SOURCE: no reordering across engines: XRT run list, /opt/xilinx/xrt/include/xrt/experimental/xrt_kernel.h:21 (XRT 2.25.0); the in-order and blocking behavior rests on the paired measurements of Section 3.1.
\textbf{Command Processor.}
The host drives the array through \emph{dispatches}, and each dispatch is a command buffer whose \emph{instruction stream} the NPU's command processor (CP) executes in order (Figure~\ref{fig:arch}).
An \emph{issue} pushes a BD into a shim DMA channel's task queue and returns at once, whereas a \emph{synchronization} blocks the CP until a named transfer completes.
A synchronization on one column therefore delays every later issue, whichever column it targets, so the CP's order decides when each column group receives work.
No hardware or runtime scheduler on XDNA~2 reorders work across engines, so that order is the array's schedule (Section~\ref{subsec:semantics}).

% VALUE: the host side: dispatches go through XRT and the driver to a hardware context, which holds one configuration and has one CP that runs them in submission order; each dispatch costs a fixed floor F, partly hidden by queuing
% SOURCE: XRT empty dispatch (4 KB bypass), 93.0-98.5 us at every bracket of lab-prefill-device (3); 92-99 us in lab-prefill-overlap (3).
\textbf{Host Runtime.}
The host submits dispatches through XRT~\citep{xrt-repo} and the amdxdna driver~\citep{xdna-driver} to a \emph{hardware context}, which holds one configuration and has one CP that runs its dispatches in submission order.
Submitting and completing a dispatch costs a fixed \emph{dispatch floor} $F$.
Queuing further dispatches before waiting on the first partly hides this floor behind the device's work.

\subsection{Modular and Fused Designs}
\label{subsec:spectrum}

% VALUE: three cuts of a design: into configurations (modular, which pays reconfiguration and runs operators in turn because a context holds one configuration on all eight columns; fused, which can run operators at once but must fit every dataflow into one configuration and queues on one CP), into dispatches, and into buffers per loop role; the three stacks we read and their one interface
% DECISION: the modularity-fusion spectrum is the author's framing (2026-10-24): modular designs trade reconfiguration time for ease of programming, fused designs avoid reconfiguration and inherit an order; neither end is called wrong. No claim about how any stack chose its order; FastFlowLM is described by what it ships.
% SOURCE: every hardware context is allocated all eight columns per the driver's source (amdxdna 2.25.0 npu4_regs.c:94-106, aie2_ctx.c:604-608; vault lab-prefill-overlap (31)); a hardware context holds its configurations one at a time (FastFlowLM's per-operator engine and IRON's operator sequences, Section subsec:pays).
% SOURCE: IRON's OperatorSequence keeps each operator its own aie.device and emits configure/run per runlist entry in runlist order (amd-iron 1fd3dab, iron/common/sequence.py:89-96, 286; iron/common/compilation/sequence.py:243-324). FastFlowLM's engines reach the runtime through libhrx and ship as compiled libraries and xclbins (FastFlowLM 44d01787, lib/hrx/libgemma4e_flash.so; vault lab-cosched-passes (14)).
A developer cuts an LLM's work at three levels, and the first cut, into configurations, places a design along a spectrum.
At the spectrum's \emph{modular} end, a design gives each operator its own configuration and reconfigures the array between operators, a cost that prior work characterizes and reduces~\citep{vandelm2026configwall}.
Because a hardware context holds one configuration at a time and the driver gives every context all eight columns, a modular design runs its operators in turn whatever their order.
At its \emph{fused} end, a design keeps several operators resident in one configuration, which avoids reconfiguration and lets operators on disjoint parts of the array run at once.
Fusing has its own cost, because the dataflows of every resident operator must then fit together into the tiles, DMA channels, buffers, and routes of one configuration.
The operators of a fused design also run from one hardware context, whose dispatches queue on one CP.
A second cut splits a fused design's work into dispatches, and a third decides whether each role in a loop keeps one buffer or several.
IRON, a close-to-metal Python interface to MLIR-AIE~\citep{hunhoff2025iron} that can also express fused designs, composes an LLM as a sequence of operators that each reconfigure the whole array, whereas AIR generates fused designs.
FastFlowLM (FLM)~\citep{fastflowlm-repo} ships fused flash designs and a modular per-operator engine as binaries with the runtime that issues them.
All three stacks reach the array through the same dispatches and instruction streams.

\subsection{LLM Inference on the NPU}
\label{subsec:prefill}

% VALUE: prefill and TTFT; the layer's operators, all GEMMs but attention; AIR's fused prefill in one configuration, the original program, the split and its supported configurations; the cores loop on runtime parameters, so operators differ only in their streams; 128-token chunks run stage by stage, attention reading earlier chunks; the host's post-processing steps between dispatches
% SOURCE: mlir-air a3e26261 programming_examples/llms/shared/fused_prefill/: device.py (column map cols(cfg); "one PDI serves every op and shape and the ops differ only in their insts"), engine.py (strip_columns), dense.py (_mix_all, stage-major order), hostops.py.
% SOURCE: mlir-air a3e26261 fused_prefill/device.py: Attn(col=...) per group in Config.attn, GCOL0, GNC = 1, 6 as module constants; spec() splits kv_heads evenly, so 1, 2, or 4 attention columns with 8 KV heads (vault lab-split-sweep (1)); logits bit-identical to the default split in every configuration on both models (lab-split-sweep (2), (4), (5)).
% SOURCE: mlir-air 44e8d8f7 programming_examples/llms/shared/fused_prefill/device.py:24-30, M = 128 rows per chunk as a module constant, TM = 32 per core tile, HR = M // TM = 4 core rows of the 6 x 4 herd; no build flag (npu-gap D4, 2026-10-25), so no chunk-size baseline exists without changing the design.
\emph{Prefill} processes a prompt to produce the first output token, and its latency is the time to first token (TTFT).
Each decoder layer applies a QKV projection, attention, an output projection, and a gated feed-forward network of gate, up, and down projections, and all but attention are matrix multiplications (GEMMs).
AIR's open fused prefill places every operator of a decoder layer in one configuration, by default with the GEMMs on columns 1--6 and attention on columns 0 and 7, and we call this design with its host program the \emph{original program}.
We name its configuration by its \emph{split}, namely the number of columns that attention takes, which is a parameter of the design's build, and each admitted value gives a \emph{supported configuration}.
An LLM with 8 KV heads admits $S_1$, $S_2$, and $S_4$, with attention on 1, 2, or 4 columns and $S_2$ the default.
The design's cores loop indefinitely on work taken from runtime parameters, so within one configuration the operators differ only in their instruction streams, each of which keeps only its own operator's columns.
The host runs each layer stage by stage over chunks of 128 tokens, a size that the design fixes, and it finishes every chunk's QKV projection before any attention and every attention before the remaining projections.
Attention on one chunk reads the QKV projections of that chunk and earlier ones.
Between dispatches, the host's CPU post-processes the operators' outputs in steps that compute the normalizations, rotary embedding, and residual additions.

% VALUE: decode is a separate fused design whose attention reads the whole context's KV cache
\emph{Decode} generates one token per step with a separate design, namely AIR's fused decode, in which every layer's attention reads the KV cache of the whole context.

% VALUE: false and true dependences defined once, the false kinds (name, order) with their sources and the rewrite that removes each; the critical-path rule (cited), which Section 3's condition refines for this NPU
% DECISION: the kinds are defined once, here, with their sources (author, 2026-10-26), and called classical; Kuck names anti and output dependences (p. 208) but no order class; renaming is Tomasulo's (p. 29, doubling); the order kind is NVIDIA's single-work-queue false dependence (Kepler GK110 whitepaper: "false intra-stream dependencies", "tailor the launch order"); "false dependence" is an established term that the paper uses and does not coin, and no claim is made about who originated the classes.
% SOURCE: Kelley and Walker, p. 317: "All the activities in a critical-path are limiting in the sense that a delay in any one of them will cause a comparable delay in the completion of the project" (verify-citations-pdf.md).
Work that waits on other work whose results it does not consume has a \emph{false dependence}; where it consumes them, the dependence is \emph{true}.
One kind of false dependence is a classical anti or output dependence~\citep{kuck1981dependence}, a \emph{name} dependence on storage that two uses need not share, which renaming removes~\citep{tomasulo1967}.
The other is a wait that the issue order alone places between independent work, like those on a GPU with a single hardware work queue~\citep{nvidia-kepler-gk110}, which we call an \emph{order} dependence and which reordering removes.
Removing a false dependence of either kind can shorten a run only where the dependence lies on the run's critical path~\citep{kelley1961critical}, and Section~\ref{subsec:question} states when it can on this NPU.
